title: Common Question Archetypes
summary: Behind dozens of different phrasings, interviewers are really asking one of a handful of things. Learn the recurring question families — conflict, failure, ambiguity, disagree-and-commit, influence, feedback — and what each is actually probing beneath the surface wording.

slides.markdown:
"Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision," "describe a conflict with a teammate," and "walk me through a time you had to push back on your manager" sound different, but they're testing the same underlying thing: how you handle disagreement. Once you recognize the archetype, wording differences stop mattering.

This topic catalogs the recurring archetypes and, more importantly, what each is *actually probing* beneath its surface phrasing — because answering the literal question is not the same as answering what the interviewer needs to hear. Pair this with your tagged story bank from the previous topic: recognizing the archetype is what lets you retrieve the right story fast.

slides.sectionTitle: Conflict with a peer or manager
slides.subTitle: What's really being tested
slides.markdown:
Surface wording: "tell me about a conflict," "a time you disagreed with a teammate," "a time you had friction with your manager."

What's actually being probed: not whether conflict happened — it always does — but **how you handled it**. Interviewers are listening for: did you address it directly rather than avoiding or escalating prematurely, did you stay professional and fact-based rather than personal, and did the relationship survive or improve afterward.

The answer that scores worst here isn't "I had no conflicts" (that's usually read as evasive or dishonest) — it's a conflict story where you're clearly still angry, where the resolution came from someone above you intervening, or where you can't say how things are with that person now. The strongest signal is a conflict you resolved yourself and a relationship that's fine today.

slides.subTitle: Why a real failure beats a humblebrag
slides.markdown:
Surface wording: "tell me about a failure," "a time something didn't go as planned," "a mistake you made."

What's actually being probed: self-awareness and whether you learn from mistakes without becoming defensive or paralyzed by them. This is one of the most-asked archetypes across every level, and one of the most commonly botched.

The fake-failure answer — "I worked too hard and burned out," "I cared too much about quality and it slowed the team down" — is a well-known pattern interviewers recognize immediately, because it's a virtue dressed as a flaw. It scores *worse* than an honest failure, because it signals you either can't identify a real mistake or won't admit to one out loud. A real failure names a genuine misjudgment, its actual consequence, and a concrete change you made afterward.

Surface wording: "a time requirements were unclear," "a project where you didn't have all the information," "how do you handle ambiguous priorities."

What's actually being probed: whether you can make forward progress and reasonable decisions without waiting for someone to hand you a complete spec — a core signal for roles above entry level, where ambiguity is the default state, not an exception.

Strong answers name the specific gap ("we didn't know whether the client wanted feature A or B"), the action taken to reduce it cheaply (a quick clarifying question, a small spike, checking with a stakeholder) rather than either freezing or guessing blindly, and how the eventual resolution came about. A weak answer treats ambiguity as something that happened *to* you rather than something you actively navigated.

slides.sectionTitle: Disagreeing with a decision and committing anyway
slides.markdown:
Surface wording: "a time you disagreed but had to go along with the decision anyway," "how do you handle a call you don't agree with."

What's actually being probed: this is deliberately a different competency from plain conflict. Interviewers want to see that you can voice real disagreement clearly, lose the argument, and then execute the decision in good faith rather than sandbagging it or relitigating it afterward — this is often called "disagree and commit" and is explicitly one of Amazon's Leadership Principles.

The trap is answering with a story where you were actually right and got vindicated, which subtly answers a different, easier question. The strongest version of this story is one where the decision genuinely could have gone either way, you made your case once clearly, and you then executed it fully — regardless of whether it turned out well.

Surface wording: "a time you got buy-in from a team you didn't manage," "how did you convince a stakeholder," "a time you drove change without formal authority."

What's actually being probed: whether you can move people toward an outcome using reasoning, credibility, and relationship-building rather than positional power — increasingly important at senior and staff levels where org charts rarely hand you the authority a decision needs.

Strong answers name the specific mechanism of influence: data that reframed the conversation, a small proof-of-concept that made an abstract idea concrete, or one-on-one alignment before a group meeting so the room wasn't hearing the idea cold. Weak answers describe the outcome ("eventually they agreed") without any mechanism, which reads as luck or seniority doing the work rather than skill.

Surface wording: "a time you gave difficult feedback," "how do you handle critical feedback about your own work," "tell me about a performance conversation."

What's actually being probed: two distinct skills often bundled in one question — can you deliver feedback that's specific and actionable without being harsh or vague, and can you receive feedback about yourself without becoming defensive.

For giving feedback, the strongest stories show a concrete, timely, private conversation with a specific behavior named and a follow-up to check it landed — not a vague "I told them to do better." For receiving feedback, the strongest stories show you actually changed behavior afterward, not just that you "took it well" in the moment. Say what changed, not just how you felt about hearing it.

slides.subTitle: "I worked too hard"
slides.markdown:
Worth isolating on its own because it's the single most common failure pattern across all archetypes, not just the failure question. Any answer that frames a virtue as a flaw — "I care too much," "I'm too much of a perfectionist," "I take on too much because I want to help" — reads as a rehearsed dodge, because interviewers hear it dozens of times a year.

It fails for a specific reason: the question is testing self-awareness, and this answer demonstrates the opposite — an inability or unwillingness to name a genuine misjudgment. A far stronger move is naming something that actually cost time, credibility, or a relationship, and being specific about what you changed afterward. Vulnerability, used carefully, reads as senior; a disguised brag reads as either naive or evasive.

A quick mental checklist for the first five seconds after a question lands, before you start speaking:

| Question mentions… | Likely archetype |
|---|---|
| "disagreement," "pushback," "friction" | Conflict, or disagree-and-commit — listen for whether the decision already happened |
| "didn't go as planned," "mistake," "failure" | Failure/growth — avoid the fake-failure trap |
| "unclear requirements," "incomplete information" | Ambiguity |
| "convince," "buy-in," "no formal authority" | Influence/leadership |
| "feedback," "performance conversation" | Giving/receiving feedback |

This mapping is what turns your tagged story bank from a list into a lookup table under time pressure — recognize the archetype, retrieve the tagged story, deliver the STAR shape.

The deeper skill this topic builds toward: treating every behavioral question as a proxy for one of a small set of underlying competencies, and answering the underlying competency rather than the literal words. An interviewer who asks "tell me about your proudest achievement" is very often still scoring ownership or scope of impact, not sentimentality.

The next few topics build directly on this: how the same competencies get relabeled by company (Amazon's Leadership Principles vs. Google's "Googleyness" vs. Meta's core values), and how your answer to the same archetype should shift as you interview for a more senior level.
